content: A traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) involves damage to the neural elements of the spinal cord, which can lead to varying degrees of sensory and motor deficits, as well as autonomic or bowel dysfunction. One of the primary rehabilitation goals for individuals with SCI is to improve their ability to walk. Locomotor training is a rehabilitation strategy aimed at enhancing walking function in these individuals. However, a systematic review of the available evidence is necessary to evaluate the effectiveness and acceptability of locomotor training after SCI. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of locomotor training on walking improvement in individuals with traumatic SCI. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including the Cochrane Injuries Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, AMED, SPORTDiscus, PEDro, COMPENDEX, and INSPEC, covering studies up to November 2011. Additionally, online trial registries such as Current Controlled Trials and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched. Relevant conference proceedings were hand-searched, reference lists of published studies were reviewed, and study authors were contacted to identify published, unpublished, and ongoing trials. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared locomotor training to either other forms of exercise or no treatment in individuals with SCI. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion, assessed their quality, and extracted data. The primary outcomes of interest were walking speed and walking capacity at the final follow-up. Five RCTs involving a total of 309 participants were included in the review. The overall findings were inconclusive. No locomotor training approach demonstrated a statistically significant advantage over other forms of physical rehabilitation in improving walking function after SCI. Specifically, bodyweight-supported treadmill training, a commonly used locomotor training method, did not significantly improve walking velocity (mean difference: 0.03 m/sec; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.05 to 0.11; P = 0.52; I² = 22%) or walking capacity (mean difference: -1.3 meters; 95% CI: -41 to 40; P = 0.95; I² = 62%). One study involving 74 participants reported that individuals receiving robotic-assisted locomotor training had reduced walking capacity compared to those receiving other interventions. This finding warrants further investigation. Across all five studies, there were no significant differences in adverse events or dropout rates between the intervention groups. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence from RCTs to determine whether any specific locomotor training strategy is superior in improving walking function for individuals with SCI. The effects of robotic-assisted locomotor training, in particular, remain unclear and require further research through large-scale RCTs. Future studies should aim to address specific questions regarding the most effective types of locomotor training for enhancing walking function in this population.
